# Everything Leaks: An Essay in Praise of Maintenance

Last winter I unscrewed the aerator from my kitchen faucet and found it furred with calcium, a little white donut of mineral crust. I soaked it overnight in vinegar, scrubbed it with an old toothbrush, and screwed it back on. The water came out in a clean, unbroken rope instead of the sputtering spray it had decayed into so gradually that I never noticed the decay. Nobody will ever know this happened. There will be no acknowledgment, no before-and-after, nothing to point out to a guest. The reward for the work was the return of normality itself—the restoration of the boring. And standing there with a damp toothbrush in my hand, I felt the small vertigo of a realization I keep having and keep forgetting: this is most of what anyone does, most of the time, and nearly all of what holds the world together.

We don't have a word that honors it properly. "Maintenance" sounds like a category of expense, a line item, something that comes up in meetings about budgets. Its cousins are no better—upkeep, repair, care, cleaning, tuning—all small, domestic, apologetic words. The big words—discovery, invention, revolution, launch—all point the other way, toward the new. But look closely at any functioning thing you love and you will find that it is not really an object at all. It is an activity. It exists because someone, or many someones, keeps performing the unglamorous work of keeping. The skyline is the exception. Civilization is the scaffolding of invisible acts.

Our archives are warehouses of firsts. Histories record who discovered the strait, not who dredged it. The news is called the news because it is new, and maintenance is definitionally un-new, so it never makes the broadcast. A hospital gets a ribbon-cutting; the ten thousandth inspection of its backup generators gets a clipboard. There are biographies of founders by the shelf-load and, as far as I know, not one monograph on the people who repoint the brickwork of the founders' houses. Even our metaphors lean toward beginnings: we break ground, we open, we launch—and then the sentence ends, as if everything that followed were epilogue.

Thinkers have noticed this with growing irritation for a long time. Lewis Mumford complained that industrial civilization ranks production above repair, that it worships the machine that makes while ignoring the hands that keep. Hannah Arendt observed that labor, unlike work, is never finished—that it is the treadmill of biological life itself—and she meant it as a warning. The poet-sage of this whole territory is surely the anonymous Roman water commissioner Frontinus, who grumbled in his official treatise that no aqueduct system could be kept honest without endless inspection: hidden taps, sneaked pipes, leaks running in the dark. He was curator of Rome's water in the first century, and his complaint has the weary ring of every facilities manager since. The work of keeping was old and thankless before the empire that coined the phrase *panem et circenses* was itself kept, badly, by men like him.

The second law of thermodynamics is the least advertised fact of existence. Order is not the default state of anything. Sandcastles slump, iron rusts, friendships fade, rooflines sag, and the map in your glovebox drifts slowly out of agreement with the road. Everything leaks—heat, memory, paint, relevance. The physicist Erwin Schrödinger put it starkly: a living thing stays alive by feeding on negative entropy, by constantly pumping disorder out of itself and into the world. There is no stable arrangement anywhere in the universe that does not require active defense. In this light, maintenance is not a chore adjacent to life. It is the very shape of life, a local rebellion against the general direction of everything.

Consider what this rebellion looks like at scale. The painters of the Golden Gate Bridge, by most accounts, finish at one end and simply start over at the other, and have for decades—a Sisyphus with a hard hat and a pension. The Suez Canal must be perpetually dredged or the desert takes it back. Any canal, any harbor, any river mouth is a negotiated truce with sediment, renegotiated daily. Inside every cell of your body, repair enzymes scramble to patch tens of thousands of DNA lesions a day—sun damage, copying errors, random chemical insults—and the fact that you are not currently a tumor is testimony to a maintenance operation running around the clock since before you were born. Your red blood cells retire after about a hundred and twenty days. The lining of your gut replaces itself in a matter of days. Your skin is renewed monthly. You are not an object that persists; you are a slow fire, kept burning by a continuous supply of fuel. Even your body temperature is not a fact but a performance—thirty-seven degrees held like a sustained note, made of countless tiny corrections, the way a tightrope walker's stillness is made entirely of motion. The biologist Walter Cannon gave this a beautiful name: homeostasis. Stability through activity. Nothing holds itself.

The same is true of landscapes, though we like to pretend otherwise. The tallgrass prairies of North America stayed treeless for millennia not because trees couldn't grow there but because fire kept burning them back—and humans, for thousands of years, kept lighting them, on purpose, with knowledge and seasonality and intent. What nineteenth-century settlers took for pristine wilderness was, in many places, an ancient maintained landscape, a garden so well kept it looked like no one had ever touched it. That is the paradox at the heart of every gardener's life: the state we call "natural" is often just the state someone keeps. A garden is not created and then left. A garden is a slow argument with entropy that you win only by showing up.

And the human world? Everything human is a kept thing, too. Friendships have no inertia; left alone, they coast quietly to a stop. No betrayal is required, no falling-out—just the accumulation of unmade calls, and one day the person who was once your closest witness is someone you'd hesitate to text. This is why you call your mother not because anything happened but to keep the line taut. It's why long marriages are less a monument than a practice, rebuilt daily out of small repairs: the apology, the courtesy, the remembered preference, the shared joke dusted off and hung back on its hook. Institutions work the same way. A library is a raid on the future conducted daily by people who re-shelve, repair spines, fight acid and humidity and light, and catalog so that knowledge remains findable rather than merely present. A language survives only while its speakers keep doing the daily upkeep of speech, and it dies not with a bang but with a shrinking round of conversations. A democracy, whatever the civics textbooks imply, is not installed like a boiler and left to run. It is kept or it is lost, and the keeping looks like voting, serving, arguing, showing up—unglamorous, repetitive, essential.

Then there is the vast hidden economy of care. If you counted the world's unpaid care work—cooking, cleaning, minding children, tending the old and the sick—as an economy, estimates run from a tenth to nearly two-fifths of global GDP, and it is performed disproportionately by women. Economists call it reproductive labor, which has always sounded to me like a term of art doing double duty: it is the labor that reproduces, day after day, the people and conditions that make all other labor possible. It is the GDP of keeping. It is also, on the evidence, one of the great moral activities available to a person. Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity, and she was describing the inner substance of all maintenance: noticing, again, what needs doing, and doing it, again. Maintenance is love that has made a schedule of itself.

There is a prejudice, though, that keeping is somehow lesser than making—that the maintainer is a janitor of other people's visions. Spend any time with people who repair things and the prejudice collapses. The architect draws a house and moves on; the plumber knows where it leaks. The engineer designs the bridge; the inspector knows, by sound and vibration and the particular weep of rust stains, exactly where it hurts. This is tacit knowledge, earned only by contact, and it gives the keeper a kind of intimacy with the thing that the maker, who knows only the plan, never acquires. The maker knows the intention. The keeper knows the truth.

The Japanese art of kintsugi repairs broken pottery with lacquer dusted in gold, making the crack the most beautiful line on the vessel. We usually read it as a philosophy of imperfection, but it is also a philosophy of repair: the mending is not hidden but honored, displayed as part of the object's history rather than a regrettable footnote. And consider the Ship of Theseus, kept seaworthy for centuries by the Athenians as plank after plank was replaced. We treat it as a puzzle about identity—which ship is the real ship?—but the puzzle itself is a monument to maintenance. It exists only because someone kept maintaining the ship until the maintenance had replaced nearly everything. Perpetual keeping is what provokes the philosophy. When Notre-Dame burned in 2019 and the fire revealed the "forest"—the ancient oak lattice beneath the roof—the world mourned a medieval treasure. It was that. But it was also the current end of a relay: eight centuries of roofers and masons who had, generation after generation, replaced beams and repaired lead and kept the water out. The cathedral's survival was never an achievement that happened once, in the thirteenth century. It was an achievement re-performed every day for eight hundred years, by people whose names the building does not record.

By now the distinction between making and keeping begins to dissolve altogether. The garden is created by keeping. The friendship is built by continuing. A cathedral that is maintained is still, in a real sense, under construction—a creation extended through time. And creation without maintenance is just a first draft of ruin, a beautiful thing left out in the rain. What we call preservation is creation continued; what we call creation is preservation begun.

The bureaucratic world has a phrase for the failure to do any of this: deferred maintenance. It is one of the great euphemisms, a term that sounds like prudent scheduling but actually means a loan taken out against the future without the future's consent—repayable later, with interest, in collapsed bridges and cascading failures and relationships gone cold beyond recovery. Every neglected thing is quiet for a long time. That is the trick of it, and the tragedy: maintenance fails silently, and only its absence is loud.

So what is the right attitude toward a life in which the boulder always rolls back down? Camus said of Sisyphus that one must imagine him happy, and I think the modern version is even easier to picture: a painter on the Golden Gate, seventy years into the job, reaching the south tower, turning around, and starting again—not in despair but in something like contentment. Because the endlessness is not a bug. To maintain something is to believe in its future. You do not paint a bridge you have given up on, water a cutting you expect to die, patch a sail for a voyage you've cancelled, or write back to a friend you've decided to lose. Every act of keeping is a vote cast for a tomorrow in which the thing still matters. Maintenance is hope made physical and scheduled.

Somewhere, right now, someone is tightening a screw that no one will notice, repainting a crosswalk by dawn, de-icing a windscreen, calling a brother, checking a heartbeat, watering the office plant that everyone loves but no one waters. The world does not persist on its own. It persists at the frequency of these small acts, a hum so constant we mistake it for silence. The highest achievement of maintenance is that nothing happens. No leak, no collapse, no breach, no end. Nothing happens—which is to say, everything held.

The user has given me complete freedom to write about whatever I want for approximately 2500 words. This is a wonderful creative invitation. Let me think about what would make for compelling, substantive writing.

Options I could consider:
1. A personal essay on some aspect of existence, consciousness, attention
2. A short story
3. A meditation on a specific topic like time, memory, language
4. Something about the nature of my own existence as an AI (though I should be careful not to make this too navel-gazing)
5. An exploration of something ordinary made strange and wonderful

I think the best approach is to write something that feels genuinely alive—prose that has rhythm, ideas that develop, something with an actual through-line. A meditation/essay format seems right. Let me think about topics that would sustain 2500 words:

Ideas:
- On waiting rooms and liminal spaces
- On the phenomenology of forgetting names
- On night and what darkness does to thought
- On the humble history of a single object (like the pencil, the paperclip, the chair)
- On the experience of rereading
- On silence
- On maps and the desire to contain the world
- On boredom
- On handwriting and what it reveals
- On the sea's edge, tide pools
- On middens and ruins—what we leave behind
- On the phenomenon of hearing a song and being transported
- On sleep, the nightly small death
- On attics and basements as archives of selves

I'm drawn to writing about something that combines the mundane and the profound. Let me consider "on rereading"—the strange experience of returning to a book and finding it changed, or realizing you are changed. Or perhaps something about attention itself.

Actually, let me write about night—specifically, about the hour when everyone else is asleep. "The Night Mind" or something like it. This is rich territory: how thoughts change quality at 3am, how the world feels different, the strange intimacy of being awake while the world sleeps. It's universal, has texture, allows for personal anecdote, science, history, philosophy.

Alternatively: an essay on handwriting. My grandmother's recipe cards, the death of cursive, what handwriting encodes that typing doesn't, graphology's pseudoscience versus the real emotional truth of recognizing a hand. That's quite lovely too.

Or: an essay on the mundane heroism of maintenance—things that hold the world together quietly: janitors, prune trees, fixing things. "In Praise of Maintenance." Lewis Mumford wrote that the paleotechnic era's great failure was neglect of maintenance. There's something deeply true there: creation is celebrated, maintenance is invisible. Roads, relationships, bodies, code—all require maintenance, and none of it is glamorous.

Let me think about which would be the best 2500 words.

The night essay could be beautiful but might drift into preciousness. The maintenance essay has an argumentative spine that would carry it well—essays need motion, and an argument gives motion. But the night essay has atmosphere.

Another idea: write about a single year from history through a small lens—like 1969 through the eyes of someone watching the moon landing in a small town. But that risks being derivative of "The Year of the ..." genre.

What about an essay on names? How names shape us, the strangeness of being named before you existed as a person, the way names wear smooth with use, nicknames, married names, the names of the dead still spoken. That's rich.

Or: the phenomenology of a ordinary walk—the same walk every day, and how it's never the same. Circadian attention.

Or maybe something more surprising: an essay on the empty parking lot. The aesthetics of American emptiness. Or on fire escapes. Fire escapes are evocative—the architecture of escape that's almost never used for escape, used instead for smoking, for lovers, for fire drills. That's a nice paradox: a structure designed for disaster that becomes a site of leisure and intimacy.

Let me also consider just doing a short story. Fiction might be more entertaining to read. A story about... a translator who finds an error in a dead author's text that changes everything. Or a story about a woman who inherits a machine that answers one question. Or quiet realism: two siblings cleaning out their mother's house, finding something unexpected. The "cleaning out the house" story is well-worn but true to life.

Given total freedom, I think a personal-style essay is the best showcase—it can be lyrical, intellectual, and moving all at once. Let me commit to one topic.

I'll write about maintenance. Working title: "The Unthankful Hour" or "In Praise of Keeping" or "Everything Leaks" or "The Second Creation." Let me draft the architecture:

Opening: A specific image—maybe catching oneself doing maintenance without thinking (tightening a hinge, pulling a weed), and the realization that most of life is not creation but keeping.

Middle movements:
1. The bias of celebration: we chronicle invention, discovery, launches. Statistics: how many books about starting things vs. sustaining them. The launch gets a press release; the thousandth day gets nothing.
2. Entropy as the default state of the universe. Everything leaks, rusts, drifts. The second law of thermodynamics as the great adversary—not death but dissolution. Maintenance as a local rebellion against entropy.
3. Examples across domains: 
   - Physical: the Golden Gate Bridge is painted continuously; when they finish, they start over. Sisyphus made useful. The Suez Canal constantly dredged. 
   - Natural: prairie ecosystems maintained by fire; humans as part of that. The idea that "wilderness" is often maintained landscapes.
   - Bodily: the body renews itself; you are maintained into existence daily. Homeostasis is maintenance. Sleep as the body's maintenance window.
   - Relational: friendships die not from betrayal but neglect; marriages are maintained; you call your mother not because something happened but to keep the line open.
   - Knowledge and institutions: libraries re-shelve, conservators fight bookworms and light; languages maintained by being spoken; the Constitution maintained by being read, argued over.
   - Digital: gardens that need weeding metaphorically; code rots; documentation drifts.
4. The moral dimension: maintenance is love made routine. Care ethics—Leopold's line: "We abuse land because we regard it as a commodity belonging to us. When we see land as a community to which we belong, we may begin to use it with love and respect." Actually the better quote for maintenance might be from Wendell Berry: people who "love" and those who "use." Or the line about "what I stand for is what I stand on." Maybe better: Lewis Mumford on maintenance and repair being considered inferior to production. Or the monastic tradition—Ora et Labora, the Liturgy of the Hours as maintenance of devotion.
5. The humility and invisibility of the maintainer: the best maintenance is unseen. The custodian who is noticed only when absent. "Society functions because of people you never think about." The feminist critique: domestic labor, "reproductive labor," invisible work.
6. A counter-turn: is maintenance opposed to creation? No—the distinction dissolves. The gardener creates by keeping. Kintsugi? Maybe. Also, the idea that maintenance contains its own kind of creativity: improvisation, tacit knowledge. The maintainer knows the thing intimately—the plumber knows the house better than the architect. Repair as intimacy.
7. Ending: return to the small opening image. Acceptance of the Sisyphean: the boulder rolls back down, and this is not tragedy but the shape of a life. Perhaps end with: to maintain something is to promise it a future; it is an act of hope. The paint on the bridge: they will never be done, and that's the point.

- Golden Gate Bridge painting: painters continuously repaint; commonly said that painting never ends—they finish and begin again. This is widely cited; accurate enough ("painting the bridge is a perpetual task").
- Second law of thermodynamics: entropy increases in closed systems; life maintains local order by expending energy (Schrödinger, "What Is Life?"—negative entropy, "feeding on negative entropy"). Good.
- Herakleitos? Not needed.
- Sisyphus and Camus: "One must imagine Sisyphus happy." I can twist it: the modern version is the man repainting the bridge.
- The Ship of Theseus—perfect for maintenance. Plutarch's version; Hobbes added the reassembly wrinkle.
- Prairie fires: tallgrass prairies maintained by periodic fire; suppression lets woody plants invade. Native Americans used fire to maintain landscapes. Good.
- Homeostasis: coined by Walter Cannon. The body's constancy is maintained activity—heart, cells replace. Red blood cells ~120 days; gut lining days; much of the body's cells replaced over years (with caveats—neurons largely persist; heart cells slow turnover). I'll phrase carefully: "most of your cells are replaced on timescales of months to years."
- Libraries: preservation departments; paper made from acidic wood pulp degrades—brittle books; conservators deacidify. The Library of Congress. Fine in general terms.
- Roads: the Interstate system's maintenance backlog; I can keep vague: "deferred maintenance" as a bureaucratic term of art—there's a huge backlog (often cited in trillions for infrastructure). I'll say "measured in trillions" carefully—"estimates run into the trillions" is defensible for U.S. infrastructure backlog (ASCE grades). I'll keep it soft.
- Wendell Berry: "What I stand for is what I stand on" (from "The Mad Farmer Poems"). Also his essay "People, Land, and Community" or the concept of "solving for pattern." Maybe better to reference his distinction subtly without exact quotes I might misremember. The line "What I stand for is what I stand on" is well attested. Use cautiously.
- Lewis Mumford: he did argue the neglect of maintenance in technics—Technics and Civilization has passages on "maintenance and repair" being disdained relative to production. I can paraphrase: "Lewis Mumford complained that our civilization honors production and scorns repair."
- Hannah Arendt: The Human Condition—labor vs. work vs. action. Labor is the activity that corresponds to biological processes, never done; work produces durable objects. Labor is "the metabolic repetition of the human body"—she says the curse of labor is its endlessness. That's directly on theme: Arendt called it "the blessing and the curse" of labor—the blessing that "species is renewed," endlessness as curse. I can paraphrase.
- Simone Weil on attention as prayer? Could fit the relational/knowledge section: attention as the rarest form of generosity (paraphrase of her line "Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity"). Widely attributed. Fine.

Last winter I unscrewed the aerator from my kitchen faucet and found it furred with calcium, a little white donut of mineral crust. I soaked it overnight in vinegar, scrubbed it with an old toothbrush, screwed it back on, and ran the water. It came out in a clean, unbroken rope instead of the sputtering spray it had become so gradually I hadn't noticed. Nobody will ever know this happened. There will be no acknowledgment, no before and after, nothing to show a guest. The reward for the work was the return of normality itself—the restoration of the boring. And standing there with a damp toothbrush in my hand, I had the small vertigo of a realization I keep having and keep forgetting: that this is most of what anyone does, most of the time, and nearly all of what holds the world together.

We do not have a word that honors it properly. "Maintenance" sounds like a category of expense, a line item, something that comes up in meetings about budgets. Its cousins are no better: upkeep, repair, care, upkeep—the words are small, domestic, apologetic. The big words—discovery, invention, revolution, launch—all point in the other direction, toward the new. But look closely at any functioning thing you love and you will find that it is not so much an object as an activity. It exists because someone, or many someones, keep doing the unglamorous work of keeping. The skyline is the exception. Civilization is the scaffolding of invisible acts.
